Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Children from a polygamist sect who one mother says are "hurting very badly" in state custody are likely to be returned to their parents, a CNN legal analyst says. FLDS member Margaret Jessop says her children "feel betrayed by adults." A Texas appeals court ruled Thursday that the state had no right to remove hundreds of children from the Fundamentalist Church of Latter-Day Saints' ranch in Eldorado on April 3, based on the suspicion that a few were being sexually abused. A sect mother who has four children in state custody said the matter has not been fully resolved because an appeal to the Texas Supreme Court is possible. "I'm very grateful, but I'd like to see the children in my arms before I rejoice greatly," Margaret Jessop said on CNN's "Larry King Live."  Watch Jessop react to the ruling » . But a permanent reunion of families is likely, said Jeffrey Toobin, CNN senior legal analyst. "Based on this ruling I think it's clear that if it stands, all these kids are going back with their mothers," Toobin said on CNN's "Anderson Cooper 360°." Jessop and other FLDS parents said they had been permitted visits with their children in foster care. Zavenda Young said two of her children were sent to Waco, Texas, and two to Hockley, 148 miles away. "They're in Boys and Girls Country in Hockley. And it's just a -- it's an institution," she told host Larry King. Their father, Edson Jessop, said the experience has been rough on the children. "You can see it's a lot of stress on them," he said. "Every time we leave, they go through that trauma again. It's enough to rip your heart out." "They feel betrayed by adults, and they're hurting very badly," Margaret Jessop added. The Texas Child Protective Services Department's Web site says the agency has been "coordinating with many professional service and government agencies to ensure the safety, health and comfort of the children and women in Eldorado." A statement from the agency Thursday said it's working out a response to the court ruling. "Child Protective Services has one duty -- to protect children," the statement said. "When we see evidence that children have been sexually abused and remain at risk of further abuse, we will act. ... We will work with the office of the attorney general to determine the state's next step in this case."

**Court finds state overstepped in largest child custody seizure in U.S. history**

An appeals court in Texas ruled Thursday that the state acted improperly when it removed more than 400 children from a polygamist sect's ranch, ordering that the children be returned to their parents.

The Third Court of Appeals in Austin found that the state Department of Family and Protective Services failed to show that the children faced imminent danger of physical harm, which is required under Texas law to justify such removals.

"The evidence presented was legally and factually insufficient to support the district court's findings," the three-judge panel wrote in its ruling.

## Background of the Case

The children were taken from the Yearning for Zion Ranch near Eldorado, Texas, in early April following an anonymous call to authorities alleging abuse. The ranch is operated by the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints (FLDS), a breakaway sect that practices polygamy and is not affiliated with the mainstream Mormon church.

State officials argued they had reason to believe the sect's practice of allowing underage girls to marry older men constituted a pervasive pattern of abuse that endangered all children on the ranch.

## The Court's Reasoning

The appeals court rejected the state's argument that the entire ranch could be treated as a single household, noting that the children lived in different family units. The judges found that the state had not demonstrated that all the children—including boys and young girls—faced the same alleged threat.

The court also noted that removing children from their homes is a severe measure that requires specific evidence of danger to each child, rather than broad assumptions about the community.

## Reactions

Attorneys representing the FLDS mothers praised the decision as a vindication of parental rights.

The Department of Family and Protective Services expressed disappointment with the ruling and indicated it was reviewing its legal options, maintaining that its actions were taken in the interest of protecting children.

## What Happens Next

The ruling directs the lower court to vacate its order placing the children in state custody. However, the case may still face further legal proceedings, and the state could appeal to the Texas Supreme Court.

The mass custody case has raised complex legal questions about the balance between protecting children from potential abuse and safeguarding the constitutional rights of parents.

# Texas Custody Case Raises Complex Legal Questions as FLDS Mothers Fight to Reunite With Children

*Legal experts weigh in on unprecedented removal of children from polygamous sect*

The custody battle involving hundreds of children removed from a West Texas ranch operated by the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (FLDS) has emerged as one of the largest and most legally complex child custody cases in American history.

State authorities removed the children from the Yearning for Zion Ranch following allegations of abuse, placing them in temporary state custody and sparking a heated debate over the balance between protecting children and preserving parental rights.

## Legal Analysis

CNN legal analyst Jeffrey Toobin characterized the case as extraordinarily difficult from a constitutional standpoint.

"This is a case that tests the limits of what the state can do," Toobin said. "The government has an obligation to protect children from abuse, but it also has to respect the fundamental rights of parents. When you're dealing with hundreds of children at once, those competing interests become enormously complicated."

Toobin noted that the sheer scale of the removal presented challenges rarely seen in family court proceedings.

"Family courts are designed to handle individual cases, examining the specific circumstances of each child and each family," he explained. "When you sweep up hundreds of children in a single action, the system strains to provide the individualized attention that due process requires."

## Voices of the Mothers

For the mothers of the sect, the removal represented a devastating separation. Speaking to reporters, several women described their anguish.

"We just want our children back," said one mother, her voice breaking. "They took our babies from us without any evidence that we did anything wrong. A mother's love is being treated like a crime."

Another woman rejected characterizations of their community as abusive.

"These are good families," she said. "Our children were happy, they were cared for, they were loved. No one has shown that my child was ever harmed in any way."

The mothers expressed particular concern about young children being separated from nursing infants and toddlers being placed with strangers.

"How can it be right to take a baby from its mother?" asked one woman. "Whatever they think about our beliefs, we are still mothers, and these are still our children."

## The Path Forward

Toobin suggested that appellate courts would likely scrutinize the state's actions carefully.

"The question isn't whether abuse occurred in some instances—it may well have," Toobin said. "The question is whether the state can justify removing every single child based on generalized allegations. Courts are generally skeptical of mass actions that don't account for individual circumstances."

He predicted the case could establish important precedents.

"However this turns out, it's going to shape how states handle situations involving closed religious communities for years to come," Toobin said. "There are no easy answers here."

As the legal proceedings continue, child welfare officials maintain they acted to protect vulnerable minors, while attorneys for the families argue the state overreached in ways that violated constitutional protections.

The case remains ongoing as courts work to determine the fate of the children and the future of the families involved.
